Messages.Body:
> My two cents is that the current errata seems to work fine and once
> newbies learn it, it becomes a accepted game mechanism.

This wasn't my point, Norm.

> There is another cards which allow you to repeatedly block with the same
> minion: Cat's Guidence.

Or you can used Forced Awakening. Again, my point wasn't about blocking
more than once with the same minion. Although, the way you suggest it, you
should use Animalism if you ever want to block.

> So if you really wanted to block with the same vamp all
> the time use animalism.

What if I want to use vamps that don't have animalsm? Just
don't expect to block?

> But, WWEF is a great card and any vampire can use it, which
> is at the heart of this arguement.

Yes and no.

> Just how much should a methuselah be able to use it without it being
> subjectively abusive?

This point could be made with just about any card in the game.

> think that if you put 20 of these in your deck that there should be a
> rather expensive opportunity cost to use them,

But where do you draw the line at being *too* expensive? 1 blood
isn't *that* much of a cost when you compare it to going an entire turn
around the table with 1 less card in your hand.I mean, hell, you can get
the blood back for _free_ in many different ways. And I'm sorry, but
a card slot is worth significantly more than a blood on a vamp. "Which
would I rather have, hmmm.... a blood on Aleph or a TelMisdirection.
That's a tough call </sar>".

> How abusive is it to use it to untap constantly?

So you are saying that Freak Drive is abusive? Or FA? Or Cat's
Guidance? Hell, I remember several games that we played when
one of us would just keep playing Cat's Guidance after a successful
block. And how is untapping constantly any more abusive than
playing, say, Telepathic Counter constantly? I seem to remember
a few of our games where I'd bleed with my minions and you would
keep Countering them. At what point did constant become abusive?

> > Why is it that the card should have heavier cost at one end of
> > the table yet have a far greater reduced (to almost nothing if
> > used at the very last action of the pred's turn) cost at the other
> > end of the table? For the *exact same opportunity*?!?

Read the above again. *This* was my point. You have a 5 player
game. You Wake during your prey's turn to attempt to block an
action. Say, equipping a mean and nasty Flame Thrower. You
are now going to have to go through 4 turns before you can redraw
the Wake. Let's say you wake during your Grand Pred's turn so you
can Eagle's Sight/Intercept a Political Action that you know is going
to be targetted at you. You now have to wait 2 turns to redraw your
Wake. Ok, now it's your Pred's turn and you Wake to block a bleed.
You now have to wait <1 turn to redraw your Wake.
How is this right? The main 2 people who you should be worrying
about blocking are your Predator and your Prey. But for the *same
opportunity* (being able to block with your tapped minion) you:

* Pay the least for Waking to block your Predator
* Pay most dearly for Waking to block your Prey
* Pay a constantly reducing cost to Wake to block those across table
from you.

Why should it be that I end up paying less to block across table than
I do to block my prey, one of those who I should be targetting? For
the exact same opportunity? It is rediculous. It is like this errata is
saying the only person you should ever be concerned about blocking
is your predator. Anyone else you are going to have to pay for. And
to top it off, we are going to tack onto that cost the fact that you are
going to be more vulnerable against your Predator if you do try to
Wake and block anyone else.
I'm sorry, but all of the above does not equal 1 blood on a vampire
by *any* stretch of the imagination. No other card in the game has
this kind of "revolving" cost. And please don't point out that in my
above examples, you should use FA instead of Wake. My point is
that the cost of Wake does not equal the cost of FA (and is in fact
significantly more expensive), which Wake was errata'd to bring more
in line with.

Sorrow

Messages.Body:
> >> So if you really wanted to block with the same vamp all
> >> the time use animalism.
> >What if I want to use vamps that don't have animalsm? Just
> >don't expect to block?

> What if I don't want to use Setites, but still expect to Corrupt people?

No, because of that little symbol there on the left that says
"Followers of Set".

> Or hit people hard using Auspex?

No, because that's not what auspex does.
Blocking, however, is a *fundamental* part of the game that *all*
vampires do and should be able to do. There is an incredibly
diverse set of options any particular vamp has open to them to
help them to block that aren't discipline based. It seems like you
are summarily dismissing all the permanents in the game because
they are not discipline based.

> There are some abilities that certain disciplines have as their asset.

Ahh, so what you are saying now is that only certain disciplines
should ever be allowed to block. I mean, my lowly KRCG isn't
worth that much against S&B so as such I shouldn't bother with
any untaps because I'm not going to block them anyways and oh
right I don't have the proper discipline to be allowed to block.
So because untapping is an ability that should have been relegated
to certain disciplines, it should be as costly as humanly possible?
</tongue in cheek sarcasm>
Having access to Wake and FA is something that all vamps
should and rightly have. I just feel that the new cost for Wake
is significantly greater than it should and needs to be.

This game is all about resource management. I am sure
everyone can agree with that (I mean, I've heard that
enough times on the NG). You have the choice of any
of the following:

* Leave minion untapped
(which a great deal of the players frown upon)
* Use FA
* Use Wake

The first means you don't do squat with the minion
against your prey, which, again, most everyone agrees
is not the best of options and is a very poor use of
resources.
The second allows you to still use your minion and try
to block your predator, but burning a blood if you fail.
Your resource utilization: minion to perform whatever
action and 1 blood if you fail to block.
The last, allows you to still use your minion and try
to block your Predator. Your resource utilization:
minion to perform whatever action and you lose a very
valuable resource (a card in your hand) regardless of
whether or not the block was successful. You are
basically trading your minion's action for a card in your
hand no matter what whereas with FA, you are trading
\your minions action for *maybe* 1 blood from that
minion. That adds up?
Plus, the amount of time varies depending on who
you attempt to block.
You lose in the first instance, you don't really lose
anything in the second instance and you lose in the
last instance, maybe even more than in the first. For all
the cries to make the game fair and balanced, I don't
see how this is either. It may be better than what was
in others' opinions, but I can hardly see how this can
be considered 'fair'.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Sorrow" <cbo...@apdi.net> writes:

>But where do you draw the line at being *too* expensive? 1 blood
>isn't *that* much of a cost when you compare it to going an entire turn
>around the table with 1 less card in your hand.I mean, hell, you can get
>the blood back for _free_ in many different ways. And I'm sorry, but
>a card slot is worth significantly more than a blood on a vamp.

I *strongly* disagree. Where that true, I would expect to see Elder
Library used a hell of a lot more than it is.

Again, it just depends on what your deck does. But I play around the
whole table with 6 card hands all the time with some of my decks. I
won't say it's not a disadvantage but I'm really confused by someone
having this much angst over the concept. (Especially when, as others
have pointed out, you only use Wake against your prey very rarely.)

To be honest, even given the errata, I originally thought it was Forced
Awakening that was the disadvantaged reaction card. I had to actually use
them in some of my decks to discover they're not so bad. (Turned out, I
overestimated how often blood actually got lost.) Perhaps you should do
the same with Wakeys? Have you used them much since the errata? Even
if so, you might want to work on "rediscovering them" deliberately in a
few decks, just to see if you're not being a bit unfair. I've found such
excersises will occasionally improve my game.

>How is this right? The main 2 people who you should be worrying
>about blocking are your Predator and your Prey. But for the *same
>opportunity* (being able to block with your tapped minion) you:
>
>* Pay the least for Waking to block your Predator
>* Pay most dearly for Waking to block your Prey
>* Pay a constantly reducing cost to Wake to block those across table
> from you.
>
>Why should it be that I end up paying less to block across table than
>I do to block my prey, one of those who I should be targetting?

Are you actually questioning such a thing? What difference does it make?
It's just part of the game. Who said it shouldn't cost more to wake to
block your prey than your predator? How did they figure out your prey
should go before your predator and everyone else ANYWAY? Is that right?
And who cares? It's just part of the game.

All that matters is that the cards are balanced to one another. This kind
of question may be a matter of taste in how the game should work. As such,
it may be legitimate to question. But this point is so picky-uny (cost of
waking to block predator vs. prey) that I have a hard time believe you
really care either way. Forgive me if your concern is legitimate, but isn't
this really just more ammo to lob at the errata for Wake? And if so, it's
not very legitimate ammo because it says nothing about whether the errata
is balanced or not.

>No other card in the game has this kind of "revolving" cost.

Forget cards, just the fact that a tapped minion can't be used to block
but an untapped minion can, and the fact that you have to tap minions to
block is the exact *opposite* effect. In short, you get to see what your
prey does with his minions actions before you're allowed to see what your
preditor does with his actions when making the decision to tap and block.
At that, your ability to block your preditor was already lower than your
ability to block your prey, since you have fewer futures actions to be
concerned about in the former case. Shouldn't *that* be a concern, also?
When did you ever object to *that* on this board?!? It's the same thing:
not all blocks are created equal. Nor were they ever intended to be. Why
are we worrying about - if not to just lob something unfair at the Wake
errata?

>My point is that the cost of Wake does not equal the cost of FA (and is
>in fact significantly more expensive), which Wake was errata'd to bring more
>in line with.

They're different in terms of quality: one is more dependent on when it's
used than the other. That, by itself, doesn't mean they're out of line
with each other. It's a deckbuilding consideration, I guess - if you expect
to block your prey more often, use FA. If you expect to block your predator
more, you may want to use Wake, instead.

Fred

Messages.Author: Derek S. Ray
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 7 Jan 2000 19:18:23 -0600, "Sorrow" <cbo...@apdi.net> wrote:

>This game is all about resource management. I am sure
>everyone can agree with that (I mean, I've heard that
>enough times on the NG). You have the choice of any
>of the following:

oo! oo! I see where I can stick my nose in!

>* Leave minion untapped
> (which a great deal of the players frown upon)
>* Use FA
>* Use Wake
>
>The first means you don't do squat with the minion
>against your prey, which, again, most everyone agrees
>is not the best of options and is a very poor use of
>resources.

Not so! A good intercept deck will leave one or several minions
untapped, so as to be able to block its prey's actions for minimal
cost. If your prey chooses to Misdirect your minions, excellent! You
have bled your prey! (And you know he's scared of you, since
Misdirection backwards is kinda rare.) So, your prey takes actions,
which you block with your untapped minions and do whatever you want in
the resulting combats. You now have a bunch of tapped minions. Now
burn your Wakes on your predator, and the card slot liability is
minimal.

If you are being hit cross-table politically, that makes it tough.
You're going to have to be a deal-maker, because almost no deck can
successfully handle two decks' offense and one deck's defense all at
the same time. Ask him why he's coming across the table in the first
place? It's usually pretty rare to have significant pool loss handed
out from, say, your grand-prey - he should be trying to keep you in so
you can pressure his predator and give him a free ride.

>The second allows you to still use your minion and try
>to block your predator, but burning a blood if you fail.
>Your resource utilization: minion to perform whatever
>action and 1 blood if you fail to block.

Meaning that approximately 20-25 cards which were designed as "free"
now cost 1 blood from a vampire. Telepathic COUNTER costs 1 blood
now, even. That starts to add up real fast. Especially if you're
Deflecting for 2 blood each time.

I prefer to use the blood on my vamps for OFFENSIVE, not defensive
purposes. FA is only suitable if you intend to be blocking a lot.

>The last, allows you to still use your minion and try
>to block your Predator. Your resource utilization:
>minion to perform whatever action and you lose a very
>valuable resource (a card in your hand) regardless of
>whether or not the block was successful. You are

This is my objection - the loss of one card in your hand is not as
valuable as you think. If you have built your deck well, you will
have a few defensive cards in hand already, so you Wake, play the
cards, replace THOSE cards, and now are down to 6. In my experience,
Wake is only a problem after you've already played 2 - finding the
defensive card to go with the third Wake is tough with only 5 cards in
hand. But this is a functional cost for a deck that surprise-untaps
constantly.

>basically trading your minion's action for a card in your
>hand no matter what whereas with FA, you are trading
>\your minions action for *maybe* 1 blood from that
>minion. That adds up?

Er, no, your minion has already TAKEN the action. You are trading a
card in your hand for the chance to take an action AND stop your
opponent. And yes, it adds up. Use FA instead of Wake when you're
not going to block sometime and see how fast those guys run out.

>Plus, the amount of time varies depending on who
>you attempt to block.
>You lose in the first instance, you don't really lose
>anything in the second instance and you lose in the
>last instance, maybe even more than in the first. For all
>the cries to make the game fair and balanced, I don't
>see how this is either. It may be better than what was
>in others' opinions, but I can hardly see how this can
>be considered 'fair'.

What's wrong with it? If you're blocking a whole lot, you're an
intercept deck and you're leaving minions untapped to begin with. If
you're only blocking critical actions, you can deal with the one-card
loss pretty easily. In your example from before, you cite a
Flamethrower equip, a nasty vote, and something your predator does.

(We're going to ignore that I'd probably let the Flamethrower go
through, just because it's a bleed for 4. For some reason you need it
blocked. Say, the vamp is Atoned and you have weenies. whatever.)

You stop the Flamethrower, and hopefully kill the vamp. Excellent
result, with future implications - you can get your bleeds in safely.
Cost: 1 card in hand for your predator's turn.

You deal-make the vote, and just absorb the damage if you can't - I
don't see actually burning Eagle's Sight for that unless you are
*really* hurting. Odds are, your predator can do worse to you than
whatever's coming cross-table, so you probably don't want to risk the
slot. This balances because you rarely ever NEED to block
cross-table.

Now, you stop your predator's worst-looking action, and maybe even a
third just-bad-looking action if you have the cards for it. No
problem for the first two, probably only small problems for the third.
If you're blocking this much, we assume your deck was designed for
it... otherwise, why are you panic-blocking this much?

-- Derek

Of course ever card should be balanced - unless you're relying on some
sort of card limits on the good cards, like restricted cards in T1 DCI
Magic construction rules. This opens the game to an additional luck
factor but some folks like that, I'm told.

Otherwise, imbalance just means people use mostly just the powerful cards,
which to me is boring and a waste of cardboard for the weaker cards.

Of course you try to balance cards. The only constroversial issues are
how far you go in pursuit of balance and how much balance do you actually
need. If you can get your balance before you print the cards, that's best.
Errataing cards causes problem distributing the errata and getting all
the players to respect the errata - or respect WotC's errata vs. their own
house rules solving the same balance problem then like better.

As for how much you really need, I think if all the different cards ever
printed play a moderate to major role in some reasonable deck archetype
(note that it's not necessary for a card to be present in a deck in large
numbers to play major role) and none of them are basically obselesced (made
into wallpaper) by another card, then you've done a great job. Most CCGs
have so many different cards printed that it's practically impossible to
do this. But if you're going to slip up, slip up by printing a few bad,
underpowered cards compared to the lot. It's the ones that are distinctly
overpowered that kill a CCG.

Fred
